To turn Node.js compatibility off, remove `"nodejs_compat"` from `compatibility_flags` in your `wrangler.toml` or `wrangler.jsonc`. Because your compatibility date is after 2024-09-23, Node.js compatibility (v2) is also enabled automatically by that date, so add `"no_nodejs_compat_v2"` to opt out of it. Then run `wrangler dev` to check the change and redeploy. Pass `--env` with the environment name, plus `--legacy-env` to deploy it as a legacy environment:

```sh
npx wrangler deploy --env staging --legacy-env
```

With legacy environments, `[env.staging]` in `wrangler.toml` produces a separate Worker named `<name>-staging`. You can also set `legacy_env = true` at the top level of the config so you don't need the flag each time. Flag and config behavior has changed across Wrangler major versions, so run `npx wrangler deploy --help` to confirm what your installed version supports.

Set the `WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS` environment variable to `false` before running Wrangler. In PowerShell, use `$env:WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS = "false"`, and in Bash, use `export WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS=false`. To make it persistent on Windows, set it through System Properties or with `setx WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS false`, which takes effect in new terminal sessions. You can also turn telemetry off with `wrangler telemetry disable`.

Use the `--jurisdiction` flag when creating the database:

```bash
npx wrangler d1 create my-database --jurisdiction eu
```

For US residency, the jurisdiction value is `fedramp` (the FedRAMP-authorized US region), so the command is:

```bash
npx wrangler d1 create my-database --jurisdiction fedramp
```

Then add the `jurisdiction` setting to your binding in `wrangler.toml` or `wrangler.jsonc` if you need it there. Jurisdiction can only be set at creation time, and it can't be changed later. Check Cloudflare's current D1 docs for the exact supported values, since I may be out of date.

Not really, at least not as a built-in deploy option. When you run `wrangler deploy`, Cloudflare updates the Worker script, and existing Durable Object instances get moved to the new code the next time they're activated, while any instance that's already running keeps its current code until it's evicted or restarts. You can't set a per-class grace period for this. The practical approaches are to keep your DO code backward compatible across deploys, or to use a version-tag pattern where the Worker routes requests to a specific class version. If you need a hard guarantee that old instances finish on old code, you'd have to handle that yourself, for example by draining or versioning the objects in your application logic.

With `wrangler dev`, `console.log` output and Wrangler's own logs print to the terminal where you started it. Nothing is written to a local log file or sent to Cloudflare, so there's no local collection to turn off. You can reduce terminal output with `--log-level` (for example `warn` or `error`), or turn off Wrangler's anonymous usage telemetry with `wrangler telemetry disable`. If you run with `--remote`, or your logs appear in the Cloudflare dashboard, that's Workers Logs/observability, which you can disable with `observability.enabled = false` in your Wrangler config. I haven't verified these flags against your installed Wrangler version, so check `wrangler dev --help` or the Wrangler docs if one doesn't behave as described.

Use `wrangler r2 sql query`, passing the warehouse name and the SQL in quotes:

Cloudflare Workflows don't have a built-in global concurrency limit setting, so the usual approach is to enforce the cap yourself. The most common way is to put a Durable Object or a KV/D1-backed counter in front of the workflow: each run acquires a slot before calling `env.MY_WORKFLOW.create()` and releases it when it finishes, rejecting or queuing requests once the limit is reached. Alternatively, if you're triggering workflows from a Queue, set the queue consumer's `max_concurrency` in `wrangler.toml` to limit how many batches are processed at once, which indirectly caps how many workflow instances start in parallel. Check the current Workflows docs for any newer platform-level limits, since this area changes often.

Not directly. Cloudflare Workers handle inbound traffic over HTTP(S) and WebSockets, so a Worker can't listen on port 5432 for raw Postgres wire protocol. Outbound raw TCP is possible through the `cloudflare:sockets` `connect()` API, which lets a Worker act as a TCP *client* to a database such as Postgres, typically with TLS. To accept raw TCP from clients, you'd need a separate server or a service like Cloudflare Spectrum or Tunnel in front of your own infrastructure, with the Worker handling only the outbound leg if needed.

The older `/__scheduled` path from Miniflare 2 has been replaced. `wrangler versions secret bulk` only adds or updates secrets from a JSON file. Leaving a key out of the file doesn't delete it, so it isn't the right command for removal. To delete a secret in a new Worker version, run `wrangler versions secret delete <SECRET_NAME>`. If your Wrangler version doesn't have that subcommand, `wrangler secret delete <SECRET_NAME>` removes it directly. I haven't checked these against your installed version, so run `wrangler versions secret --help` to confirm the available subcommands.

Yes, once you have a stub, you can call its public methods directly over Workers RPC. One correction: `newUniqueId()` returns a `DurableObjectId`, not a stub. Get the stub with `env.MyAgent.get(id)`, then call methods like `await stub.someMethod(args)`. Methods must be public and take and return serializable values. The `@callable()` decorator only controls which methods clients can reach over WebSocket, so it isn't needed for stub RPC.

A scheduled callback receives only the **payload** you passed when you created the schedule. With `this.schedule(when, "callbackName", payload)`, the agent calls `callbackName` with that payload as its single argument. The payload can be any JSON-serializable value, and it's omitted if you didn't provide one. The callback doesn't receive the schedule ID or other metadata.

The first message is an MCP `initialize` JSON-RPC request. It carries the client's supported protocol version, its capabilities, and its `clientInfo` (name and version). After the server responds with its own version and capabilities, the client sends a `notifications/initialized` notification before making other requests such as `tools/list`. This follows the MCP specification, which the Cloudflare Agents SDK implements. The test can pass even when the promise resolves to the wrong value. Without `await` (or `return`), the test function finishes before the assertion settles, so Vitest records it as passed. If the assertion later fails, the error surfaces outside the test's result, usually as an unhandled rejection that may be attributed to another test or reported only as a warning. Add `await` or `return` before `expect(...).resolves`. The ESLint rule `vitest/valid-expect` catches this pattern, and `expect.assertions(n)` helps ensure assertions actually ran.

No, Vitest doesn't walk up the directory tree to find a config. It looks for `vitest.config.*` (or `vite.config.*` as a fallback) in the current working directory, which becomes the project root. If you run it from a subfolder that has no config, it runs with defaults, so your aliases, plugins, and `include` patterns from the parent config won't apply. To fix this, run from the parent directory, pass the config explicitly with `npx vitest --config ../vitest.config.ts`, or set `--root ..`.

Probably not. `@vitest/runner` is already installed as a dependency of `vitest`, and its APIs (`test`, `describe`, `expect`, hooks) are re-exported from `vitest`, so importing from `vitest` in your tests is the normal route. Add `@vitest/runner` directly only if you import it from source code outside your test setup, such as a custom runner or reporter. In that case, pin it to the same version as `vitest` to avoid mismatches.

Install the packages `vitest`, `@vitest/browser`, and `webdriverio`, then set the `provider` in your Vitest config. In `vitest.config.ts`, import `webdriverio` from `@vitest/browser/providers/webdriverio` and set `browser: { enabled: true, provider: webdriverio(), instances: [{ browser: 'chrome' }] }` (the `instances` array is required in Vitest 3+ to name the browser). Vitest will then launch the browser through WebdriverIO's driver, and you can run tests with `npx vitest`. Check the Vitest browser mode docs for any options that differ in your installed version.

Yes. `toHaveTextContent` with a string argument checks whether the element's normalized text content *contains* that string, so it is a substring match. To require an exact match, pass an anchored regex such as `toHaveTextContent(/^Save$/)`. Whitespace is normalized by default, and you can disable that with `{ normalizeWhitespace: false }`. This matcher comes from `@testing-library/jest-dom`, so it works in Vitest only after that package is set up.

By default, `vitest --reporter=blob` writes its blob report files to a `.vitest-reports` directory in the project root. You can change the location with the `--outputFile` option. I haven't checked this against the installed Vitest version in this workspace, so confirm it with the docs for your version if the exact path matters.

Yes. Vitest browser mode's `getByText` is built on Playwright's locator semantics, so by default it matches substrings and ignores case. Pass `{ exact: true }` to require a full, case-sensitive match of the text content.

Vitest's `-t` flag matches against the full test name, which includes the enclosing describe names joined by spaces. So you pass the full path, or just a regex that matches it, for example `npx vitest run -t "outerDescribe innerTest"`. You can also pass a partial pattern like `npx vitest run -t "innerTest"`, since `-t` is a substring/regex match on the full name. Quote the pattern in PowerShell so the spaces are kept as one argument.

If the function never produces a value that satisfies the matcher, `expect.poll` fails once the timeout (default 5 seconds) elapses. The test fails with a timeout error that includes the last value the function returned, which is usually the quickest clue to why the condition never held. If the function itself hangs and never settles, I'd expect the timeout to still bound the wait and fail the test, but I haven't verified that against the Playwright source, so check the version you're using if that case matters.

No, inline projects don't inherit options from the root Vitest config. Each entry in `test.projects` is resolved as its own configuration, so settings like `environment`, `globals`, `setupFiles`, or `plugins` must be repeated in each project that needs them. Root-level options such as `coverage` and `reporters` apply to the whole run, not to individual projects. I'm answering from memory of Vitest's behavior, not from your repo, so check the Vitest docs for your installed version if the exact inheritance rules matter.

**No, not reliably.** Vitest hoists `vi.mock` calls to the top of their scope, before imports, so a call nested in a function or `if` block doesn't behave as written. For conditional mocking, use `vi.doMock`, which isn't hoisted, and then `await import(...)` the module afterward. Call `vi.resetModules()` between cases so the module is re-evaluated with the new mock, and use `vi.doUnmock` to remove a mock.

Use `mockImplementation` and branch on the arguments. For example: `const fn = vi.fn((id) => (id === 1 ? 'a' : 'b'))`, or on an existing mock: `mock.mockImplementation((arg) => { if (arg === 'x') return 1; return 2; })`. If you only need specific calls, you can chain `mockReturnValueOnce` for each call in order, or use `mockImplementationOnce`. For objects or complex arguments, compare with a deep-equality check such as `expect.objectContaining` isn't applicable here, so use your own comparison (e.g., `JSON.stringify(arg)`) inside the implementation.

Vitest has a `--repeats` option (added in v2.x/3.x) that reruns each test in the file multiple times within a single run, e.g. `npx vitest run --repeats 10`. For repeats across full runs, you can loop from the shell, such as PowerShell: `1..10 | ForEach-Object { npx vitest run }`, and stop on the first failure. Adding `--sequence.shuffle` helps surface order-dependent flakiness. Check `npx vitest --help` for the exact flags supported by your installed version.

I don't believe Vitest defines a short alias for `--project`, so you'd use the full `--project <name>` form. I'm not certain for every version, though. Running `npx vitest --help` in your project will show the exact flags your installed version supports.

Yes, but only partly. `vitest list` imports your test files so it can register the `describe`/`test` blocks, which runs any top-level code in those files. It doesn't execute the test bodies, so it prints test names without running assertions or hooks. If you pass `--filesOnly`, it lists just the matching test files without collecting individual tests.
